title: Problem Statement and Imports
content: The header states Erdős Problem #101: given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no five collinear, is the number of lines through exactly four points $o(n^2)$? This is an open problem with a $100 prize. The formalization imports Mathlib's finite set cardinality and basic natural number machinery.
mathContext: The problem asks whether $f_4(n) = o(n^2)$, where $f_4(n)$ is the maximum number of 4-point lines determined by $n$ points in general position (no five collinear). The quantity $f_4(n)$ lies between $\Omega(n^{3/2})$ and $O(n^2)$.

title: No Five Collinear Condition
content: The point set has no five collinear points: for any five distinct points $a, b, c, d, e$ in $P$, it is not the case that $a, b, c$ and $a, b, d$ and $a, b, e$ are all collinear. This is the natural threshold condition because allowing five collinear points trivially produces $\Omega(n^2)$ four-point lines by placing $\Theta(n)$ points on $\Theta(n)$ concurrent lines.
mathContext: The condition states $\forall \{a, b, c, d, e\} \subseteq P$ with all points distinct, $\neg(\text{collinear}(a,b,c) \land \text{collinear}(a,b,d) \land \text{collinear}(a,b,e))$. Equivalently, every line contains at most four points of $P$.

title: Collinearity via Signed Area
content: Three points $p, q, r$ are collinear if and only if the signed area determinant vanishes. This is the standard algebraic characterization: the cross product of displacement vectors $(q - p)$ and $(r - p)$ is zero.
mathContext: Collinearity is defined by $(q_1 - p_1)(r_2 - p_2) = (r_1 - p_1)(q_2 - p_2)$, which is equivalent to the vanishing of $\det \begin{pmatrix} q_1 - p_1 & r_1 - p_1 \\ q_2 - p_2 & r_2 - p_2 \end{pmatrix} = 0$.

title: Four-Point Line Count
content: Counts lines passing through exactly four points of $P$ by filtering 4-element subsets of $P$ that are collinear. A subset $S$ of size 4 contributes if there exist two points $a, b \in S$ such that every point $p \in S$ satisfies $\text{collinear}(a, b, p)$. This is marked `noncomputable` since it involves decidability over real-valued predicates.
mathContext: The four-point line count is $f_4(P) = |\{S \in \binom{P}{4} : S \text{ is collinear}\}|$. Note this counts 4-element collinear subsets, not lines; each line through exactly 4 points contributes exactly $\binom{4}{4} = 1$ such subset, while a line through $k \geq 5$ points would contribute $\binom{k}{4}$ subsets—but the no-five-collinear condition prevents $k \geq 5$.

title: Erdős Problem #101: The Main Conjecture
content: The central open problem: the four-point line count is $o(n^2)$, formalized as for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $N_0$ such that for all no-five-collinear point sets $P$ with $|P| \geq N_0$, we have $f_4(P) < \varepsilon \cdot |P|^2$. This is recorded as a documentation comment, not an axiom — the file declares zero axioms. The conjecture remains open (carrying a $100 Erdős prize), while the surrounding theorems prove unconditional partial bounds ($f_4 \leq n^2$, $\leq n(n-1)/2$, $\leq n(n-1)/12$, and $\leq (n-1)/3$ per point).
mathContext: The conjecture is $f_4(n) = o(n^2)$: $\forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists N_0 \in \mathbb{N}, \forall P$ with $\text{NoFiveCollinear}(P)$ and $|P| \geq N_0$: $f_4(P) < \varepsilon \cdot |P|^2$.

title: Grünbaum's Lower Bound Construction
content: Grünbaum constructed no-five-collinear point sets achieving $\Omega(n^{3/2})$ four-point lines. The construction uses points on a family of algebraic curves (specifically, unions of lines in a grid-like arrangement) that create many collinear quadruples while avoiding five-point collinearities. Erdős originally conjectured $\Theta(n^{3/2})$ was the true order of growth based on this construction.
mathContext: There exists $c > 0$ such that for all $N$, there is a set $P$ with $|P| \geq N$, $\text{NoFiveCollinear}(P)$, and $f_4(P) \geq c \cdot |P|^{3/2}$.

title: Solymosi–Stojaković: Nearly Quadratic Lower Bound
content: Solymosi and Stojaković achieved a breakthrough by constructing point sets with $n^{2 - O(1/\sqrt{\log n})}$ four-point lines while maintaining the no-five-collinear condition. This disproved Erdős's conjecture that $\Theta(n^{3/2})$ was the correct order, pushing the known lower bound tantalizingly close to the conjectured $o(n^2)$ upper bound. Their construction uses combinatorial number-theoretic techniques.
mathContext: For all $C > 0$, for all sufficiently large $n$, there exists $P$ with $|P| = n$, $\text{NoFiveCollinear}(P)$, and $f_4(P) \geq n^{2 - C/\sqrt{\log n}}$. Since $C/\sqrt{\log n} \to 0$, this is $n^{2 - o(1)}$, i.e., super-polynomial in $n$ but still sub-quadratic.

title: Trivial Quadratic Upper Bound
content: Any set of $n$ points determines at most $\binom{n}{2} = n(n-1)/2$ lines (each pair of points defines a unique line), so the four-point line count is trivially $O(n^2)$. The open question is whether this can be improved to $o(n^2)$.
mathContext: $f_4(P) \leq \binom{|P|}{2} = \frac{|P|(|P|-1)}{2}$, since each four-point line is determined by any pair of its points, and distinct pairs determine distinct lines.

title: Collinear Triples Without Four-Point Lines
content: Burr, Grünbaum, and Sloane, as well as Füredi and Palásti, constructed point sets with approximately $n^2/6$ collinear triples but no four-point lines at all. This shows that three-point collinearity can be abundant even when four-point collinearity is absent, highlighting the delicate combinatorial transition from 3-point to 4-point collinearity.
mathContext: There exist configurations $P$ with $|P| = n$, no four collinear points, and $\Theta(n^2)$ collinear triples. The constant $1/6$ comes from the construction: $\sim n^2/6$ collinear triples in $n$ points on a cubic curve.

title: Szemerédi–Trotter Incidence Theorem
content: The Szemerédi–Trotter theorem (1983) bounds point-line incidences: given $n$ points and $m$ lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$, the number of incidences is $O(n^{2/3}m^{2/3} + n + m)$. This is tight and serves as the fundamental tool in incidence geometry. For Problem #101, it provides an avenue to bound four-point lines by relating them to incidence counts.
mathContext: The Szemerédi–Trotter bound: $I(P, L) \leq C(|P|^{2/3}|L|^{2/3} + |P| + |L|)$ for some absolute constant $C > 0$. Each four-point line contributes 4 incidences, so $4 f_4 \leq I(P, L)$, but the lines $L$ depend on $P$, making direct application subtle.
